22.text: The females calve from the middle of March till the breaking-up of the

23.text: ice; i. e., the end of May. The fawns, after a few days, begin to dig for

24.text: moss. They are weak, and sensitive to frost and hunger; and hundreds of

25.text: them perish under unfavorable conditions (in the average year, about fifteen

26.text: per cent). The wild reindeer calves two or three weeks later, in accordance

27.text: with its later rutting-season. This is favorable for the fawns, which do not

28.text: perish in such numbers as in the domesticated herds. During calving-time

29.text: the herdsmen resort to an open place well sheltered from north winds, and

30.text: with little snow; as otherwise the females will lack milk, and the fawns will

31.text: be starved. In all the larger herds the pregnant females, before calving, are

32.text: separated from the bucks, harness-animals, etc.; and each part of the herd is

33.text: pastured on separate grounds. Otherwise the bucks would injure the fawns

34.text: in their runs, which occur several times a day. The two parts of the herd

35.text: are joined again late in summer, or in the fall of the year, when they are

36.text: returning from the summer pastures. The reindeer-doe begins to rut when one

37.text: year old; but some begin in the same year in which they were born. The

38.text: more favorable the summer, the more frequent will be the cases of half-grown

39.text: fawns beginning to rut. I was told by the herdsmen of the American Govern-

40.text: ment herd on St. Lawrence Island, that, on account of the rich moss-pastures
